questions.q: What is the key question to ask before choosing a join type?
options: Is the data numeric or text?
How many columns does each table have?
Which table was created first?
Do I need rows that have no match on the other side?
questions.explain: This single question routes most decisions to INNER, LEFT, FULL OUTER, or CROSS JOIN.

questions.q: For 'every customer, including those who've never ordered, with $0 shown for their spending,' which join is correct?
options: INNER JOIN, since it's simpler
LEFT JOIN, keeping every customer even without a matching order
CROSS JOIN, to get every possible combination
RIGHT JOIN, since orders come second in the query
questions.explain: "Including customers who've never ordered" is the signal that unmatched left-side rows must be kept — that's LEFT JOIN.

questions.q: Which join type would you use when you genuinely want every combination of two sets, not a match at all?
options: OUTER APPLY
SELF JOIN
CROSS JOIN
INNER JOIN
questions.explain: CROSS JOIN is rare but correct when the goal really is 'every possible pairing,' like a full size/color variant matrix.

questions.q: According to this course's convention, which should you write when you need to keep unmatched rows from one specific table?
options: LEFT JOIN — even though RIGHT JOIN could technically achieve the same result
RIGHT JOIN, always
FULL OUTER JOIN, to be safe
CROSS JOIN
questions.explain: This course consistently prefers LEFT JOIN (Lesson 24) for readability, even though RIGHT JOIN is a valid alternative.

questions.q: When does CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY come into play instead of a regular JOIN?
options: Only when using SELF JOIN
Whenever WHERE is also present in the query
Whenever more than two tables are involved
When joining to a table-valued function rather than a table, needing per-row re-evaluation
questions.explain: APPLY exists specifically for joining to functions that need each row's own value as input, which regular JOIN...ON cannot do.
